healthcare: I would use a hybrid deployment: a community cloud restricted to participating hospitals for identifiable patient data and clinical analytics, connected to a public cloud for the SaaS frontend and approved de-identified workloads. Hospitals with stricter requirements can retain records in private clouds and exchange only authorised data. The community tier supports shared governance; the public tier supplies elastic capacity. SaaS is the service offered to hospitals, while community, private and public describe deployment models. [1]

The protected tier would enforce hospital-level tenancy, federated identity, least-privilege roles, encryption in transit and at rest, controlled key access, data residency, retention rules and auditable access. Every request must carry a verified tenant identity. De-identification and release checks must precede transfer to the public tier. Sensitive workloads remain protected during outbreaks; provider certifications complement application controls and hospital agreements.

I would scale stateless APIs horizontally behind a load balancer using request rate and latency, buffer ingestion bursts in queues, and scale analytics workers with backlog. Partition data by hospital and region, cache suitable aggregates and apply tenant quotas. Replicate services across availability zones, test recovery, and pre-warm critical capacity before expected surges. National expansion adds regional deployments within residency rules. Private/community capacity requires advance provisioning: public-cloud bursting is limited to workloads approved for that environment.
bank: I would choose PaaS on a private cloud dedicated to the bank, with a hybrid transition while legacy services remain on premises. PaaS supplies managed runtimes, deployment automation and platform maintenance while the bank controls application logic and data. A private deployment supports exclusive access, deliberate data placement and audit requirements. PaaS is the service model; private/hybrid are deployment models. A VPC in a public cloud alone does not make that environment a private cloud under the NIST definition. [1]

Modernise incrementally through stable APIs, staged replacement and data reconciliation. Use IaaS temporarily when legacy dependencies require operating-system control. Keep regulated records in the approved private environment and allow public services only for authorised workloads. Enforce separation of duties, controlled encryption keys, private connectivity, immutable audit records, tested recovery and retention rules. Validate provider evidence, contracts, jurisdiction and outsourcing obligations with the bank's compliance team. The tradeoff is greater cost and capacity planning than shared public PaaS, balanced by isolation and control.
frontend_setup: The frontend uses HTML, CSS and JavaScript stored in private S3. A Lambda asset handler serves these files through API Gateway over HTTPS. Same-origin fetch requests call /api endpoints to display the required users, searchable and paginated statistics, sorting, and CSV export.
backend_setup: API Gateway routes /api requests to a Python Lambda function and website requests to a separate Lambda asset handler. An analysis controller uploads the dataset and PySpark script to S3, launches a three-node EMR cluster running Spark on YARN, validates the completed step and results against an independent SQLite reference, then publishes a compressed snapshot. The API Lambda reads private S3 results, caches them for 30 seconds, and serves summary and user statistics. IAM roles restrict storage access; the EMR cluster terminates after its step finishes.
analysis_description: Amazon EMR on EC2 runs Spark 3.5.2 on YARN using EMR release 7.5.0. [2,3] The cluster has an on-demand primary, an on-demand core worker and a Spot task worker, all m5.xlarge. Two 8 GiB executors process the S3 input across separate workers. Spark validates rows, deduplicates directed edges and aggregates followers by target and followees by source. It writes partitioned user results, audit totals and executor evidence to a new S3 run directory. Publication requires a completed step, all three success markers, tasks completed on two distinct worker hosts and agreement with the independent reference. The cluster terminates after its step.
